items.title: UK net migration falls to 77,000, lowest since 1997 excluding Covid pandemic – UK politics live
items.desc: Net migration fell in the year ending June 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics The Liberal Democrats are saying the UK needs a proper plan for immigration. This is from the party’s asylum and immigration spokesperson, Paul Kohler . Britain needs to regain control of its immigration system after the chaos of Brexit. Yet sixteen years after David Cameron’s ‘tens of thousands’ pledge, six prime ministers and ten home secretaries have overseen wild swings in immigration numbers with net migration now set to fall below zero. Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services. The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.

When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?, 24 November ), is the expression of the overwhelming momentum of the value system of a global culture that is wedded to the seemingly unstoppable expansion of our material production and consumption. The disjunction between peril and necessary action is explained by the impossibility of taming appetites that are insatiable. It is convenient to blame fossil fuel producers, and while they are obviously guilty parties, the ultimate problem is the continuing demand for their products. Continue reading...

items.title: Energy bills jump: how to switch providers and is it worth it?
items.desc: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the 26% price rise in January Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain will go up by 26% in January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year. However, your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. On Wednesday, the cheapest fixed tariff on the market, an 18-month fix from Fuse Energy, was priced at £1,754 for an average home – £412 below the new January cap. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use. Continue reading...
